s: Mencius (2A6) names the heart of approving and disapproving (是非之心) as the sprout or starting-point (端) of zhi 智, one of four moral beginnings every person has like four limbs, to be extended and filled out.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: The feeling of approving and disapproving is the principle of knowledge.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: 是非之心、智之端也

s: Mencius (6A15) contrasts the senses, which do not think and are led away by things, with the heart-mind, whose office (官) is to think (心之官則思); both are given by Heaven, and standing first in the greater part keeps the lesser from taking over.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: The senses of hearing and seeing do not think, and are obscured by external things. When one thing comes into contact with another, as a matter of course it leads it away. To the mind belongs the office of thinking.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: 耳目之官不思而蔽於物物交物則引之而已矣心之官則思思則得之不思則不得也

s: Mencius (7A1) holds that one who exhausts (盡) his heart-mind knows his nature, and knowing his nature knows Heaven: the full exercise of xin is the route to the cosmic order.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: He who has exhausted all his mental constitution knows his nature. Knowing his nature, he knows Heaven.

s: Mencius (7A15) calls the knowledge people have without deliberating (不慮而知) their liangzhi 良知, instanced by infants loving parents and children respecting elders; Legge renders it 'intuitive knowledge'.

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: the knowledge possessed by them without the exercise of thought is their intuitive knowledge

src.l: Mencius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 2: The Works of Mencius
src.q: 所不慮而知者、其良知也

s: Xunzi (Jiebi, ch. 21) calls the heart-mind the lord of the body's form and master of spirit-like intelligence (神明之主): it issues commands and receives none, and while mouth and body can be forced, it cannot be forced to change its judgment.

src.l: Xunzi, Homer H. Dubs (trans.), 1928, The Works of Hsüntze
src.q: The mind is the ruler of the body and the master of the spirit. It gives commands and all parts of the body obey.

src.l: Xunzi (荀況), Yang Liang (楊倞), commentary, n.d., 荀子·卷十二~卷十六 (vol 4), with Yang Liang's commentary
src.q: The heart-mind is the lord of physical form and the master of divine illumination. It issues commands but receives no command from anything else.
src.qo: 心者形之君也而神明之主也出令而無所受令

s: Xunzi (Jiebi) answers 'how does the heart-mind know [the Way]?' with: by being empty, unified and still (虛壹而靜); each quality coexists with its opposite, since the mind always stores, always holds more than one thing, and always moves.

src.l: Xunzi (荀況), Yang Liang (楊倞), commentary, n.d., 荀子·卷十二~卷十六 (vol 4), with Yang Liang's commentary
src.q: How does the heart-mind know? I say: through emptiness, unity, and stillness.

src.l: Xunzi (荀況), Yang Liang (楊倞), commentary, n.d., 荀子·卷十二~卷十六 (vol 4), with Yang Liang's commentary

s: Zhuangzi (ch. 4) has Confucius teach the 'fasting of the heart-mind' (心齋): make the will one, listen not with the ears but the mind, then not with the mind but with qi, which is empty and waits on things; the Dao gathers only in emptiness, and emptiness is the fasting of the heart.

src.l: Zhuangzi (莊周), 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 1
src.q: Do not listen with your mind, but listen with your qi … Qi is empty and waits for things. Only the Dao gathers in emptiness.
src.qo: 無聽之以心而聽之以氣

src.q: 無聽之以心而聽之以氣

src.q: You will not wait even for the hearing of your mind, but for the hearing of the spirit.

s: Zhuangzi (ch. 7) says the perfect man uses his mind like a mirror: it neither escorts nor anticipates things, responds without retaining, and so deals with all things without injury.

src.l: Laozi, Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39): Tao Te Ching; Kwang-sze Books I-XVII
src.q: When the perfect man employs his mind, it is a mirror. It conducts nothing and anticipates nothing; it responds to (what is before it), but does not retain it. Thus he is able to deal successfully with all things, and injures none.

src.l: Zhuangzi, Herbert A. Giles (trans.), 1889, Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
src.q: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing : it refuses nothing.

s: The Daodejing (ch. 18-19) treats wisdom (智) as a symptom of the Dao's decline, appearing with hypocrisy once the great Dao is lost, and advises renouncing sageness and discarding wisdom for the people's benefit.

src.l: Laozi, Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39): Tao Te Ching; Kwang-sze Books I-XVII
src.q: When the Great Tâo (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue. (Then) appeared wisdom and shrewdness, and there ensued great hypocrisy.

src.l: Laozi, Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39): Tao Te Ching; Kwang-sze Books I-XVII
src.q: If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it would be better for the people a hundredfold.

s: Daodejing 33 ranks self-knowledge above knowledge of others: knowing others is 'discerning', knowing oneself is 'intelligent' (Legge), the pair usually given as 智 and 明.

src.l: Laozi, Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39): Tao Te Ching; Kwang-sze Books I-XVII
src.q: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.

s: Analects 2.17 defines knowing (知) reflexively: to hold that you know what you know and allow that you do not know what you do not know, this is knowing.

src.l: Confucius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1: Confucian Analects, The Great Learning, The Doctrine of the Mean
src.q: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge.

src.l: Confucius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1: Confucian Analects, The Great Learning, The Doctrine of the Mean
src.q: 知之為知之不知為不知是知也

s: The Great Learning places the extension of knowledge (致知) through the investigation of things (格物) at the root of a chain: knowledge made complete makes thoughts sincere, then the heart rectified, then person, family, state.

src.l: Confucius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1: Confucian Analects, The Great Learning, The Doctrine of the Mean
src.q: Wishing to be sincere in their thoughts, they first extended to the utmost their knowledge. Such extension of knowledge lay in the investigation of things.

src.l: Confucius, James Legge (trans.), 1893, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1: Confucian Analects, The Great Learning, The Doctrine of the Mean
src.q: 欲誠其意者先致其知致知在格物

s: The Shujing ('Counsels of the Great Yu') warns that the human heart is precarious and the heart of the Way is subtle, and enjoins being discriminating and undivided (惟精惟一) so as to hold fast the mean.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1865, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 3, Part 1: The Shoo King
src.q: The mind of man is restless,—prone to err; its affinity for the right way is small. Be discriminating, be undivided

s: A commentator quoted in Legge's Shujing (Great Declaration) holds that man alone receives the energizing qi complete, which makes human nature uniquely ling 靈 among creatures, but most cannot preserve it and need an intelligent ruler-parent so the people can 'complete their intelligence'.

s: Zhuangzi (ch. 23 in Legge's numbering) speaks of a 'Tower of Intelligence' with a Guardian who acts unconsciously and whose care fails if there is conscious purpose; Legge's note identifies this Guardian of the mind with the Tao.

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 2 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 40)
src.q: That Tower has its Guardian, who acts unconsciously, and whose care will not be effective, if there be any conscious purpose in it

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part 2 (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 40)
src.q: This Guardian of the Mind or Tower of Intelligence is the Tâo.

s: Wang Yangming (Henke's translation) holds that all seeing, hearing and daily dealings fall within the single task of extending intuitive knowledge (致良知) to the utmost, so that 'the task is but one'.

src.l: Wang Yangming, Frederick G. Henke (trans.), 1916, The Philosophy of Wang Yang-ming
src.q: there is nothing which is not the result of the progressive manifestation of the intuitive faculty. Eliminate the experiences of mutual intercourse, and thereby the development of the intuitive faculty is made impossible. For this reason the task is but one.

s: Critique: the Daoist texts press against 'intelligence is the harmonizing' and against intelligence as a value at all: the Laozi treats 智 as a symptom of lost harmony, and Zhuangzi's highest mind is an emptied mirror that responds without retaining or integrating; harmony there comes from subtracting the mind's work, not from its coordinating activity.

src.q: The first of which is that they could never use words, nor other signs in composing them, as we do to declare our thoughts to others.

s: In Meditation II Descartes answers 'what am I?' with 'a thinking thing' (res cogitans), which he spells out as a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, imagines and senses, so that will and sense fall under cogitatio.

src.q: But what, then, am I? A thinking thing . What is that? It is a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, and also imagines and senses.

s: Leibniz (Monadology §17) argues that if a machine that thinks and perceives were enlarged so one could walk into it as into a mill, one would find only parts pushing one another and nothing to explain a perception; so perception must be sought in a simple substance, not in a machine.

src.q: one might go into it as into a mill. … find only parts which work one upon another, and never anything by which to explain a perception … in a simple substance, and not in a compound or in a machine, that perception must be sought for

s: Hersent's 1626 commentary on Dionysius' Mystical Theology reasons that since for Dionysius and the Platonists God is not a being but above being, God is above the intelligible and the intellect and so 'cannot be called intelligible, but superintelligibilis': the Dionysian super- prefix applied to the vocabulary of understanding.

src.l: Charles Hersent, 1626, In Dionysii Areopagitae De mystica theologia
src.q: liquidò constat Deum esse supra intelligibile & intellectum: vnde intelligibilis dici non potest, sed superintelligibilis.

François Chollet, 2019, On the Measure of Intelligence

s: A small literature sets Aquinas's angels beside AI: Kainz (1998) notes parallels between computer mechanisms and Aquinas's metaphysics of angelic faculties, and Haselager (2024) proposes comparing humans with 'animals, angels, and AI' in a newly extended great chain of being, inspired by Aquinas; both argue by analogy of faculties, not by descent of the word.

src.l: Howard P. Kainz, 1998, Artificial Intelligence and Angelology
Pim Haselager, 2024, From Angels to Artificial Agents? AI as a Mirror for Human (Im)perfections

s: Chua Soo Meng (2001) argues that Aquinas's account of angels as cognitively intuitive and non-discursive makes the analogical gap between computers and the Thomistic separate substances impossible to bridge, and points away from computers as the way up the order of cognitive excellence.

src.l: Jude Chua Soo Meng, 2001, Artificial Intelligence and Thomistic Angelology: a Rejoinder

s: Geraci (2008) reads popular robotics and AI writing as a merger of Jewish and Christian apocalypticism with science: alienation in this world, a heavenly new world, and transformed purified bodies, here a virtual world of intelligent machines and humans uploaded into machines.

s: Interpretive: none of the founding texts read (Dartmouth 1955, Good 1965 as quoted by Vinge, Vinge 1993, Bostrom 1998) mentions angels, the medieval Intelligences or Dionysius, and the scholarship found links angels and AI only by analogy (Kainz, Haselager, Chua) or links AI to apocalypticism (Geraci); so 'superintelligence' inherits the older sense at most in grammar (an intelligence as an entity) and in ranking above humans, while inverting its content: the medieval higher intellect is higher by not reasoning, the modern one by reasoning better.

s: Al-Kindī's treatise On the Intellect, in its medieval Latin version, divides intellect into four species: the intellect always in act, the intellect in the soul in potency, the intellect that has passed in the soul from potency to act, and a fourth he calls 'demonstrative'.

src.l: al-Kindī, 1897, Die philosophischen Abhandlungen des al-Kindi
src.loc: Liber Alkindi de intellectu, opening; ed. p. 5 [scan 42]
src.q: But their opinion is that the intellect is according to four species. The first is the intellect that is always in act. The second is the intellect that is in the soul in potentiality. The third is the intellect when it exits in the soul from potentiality to effect.
src.qo: sed sententia eorum est, quod intellectus est secundum quatuor species. prima est intellectus qui semper est in actu. secunda est intellectus qui in potentia est in anima. tertia est intellectus cum exit in anima de potentia ad effectum.

s: The 1897 editor of al-Kindī's treatises reads On the Intellect as perhaps the first Arabic statement of the doctrine later found in al-Fārābī and finished by Ibn Rushd, and glosses its four intellects with the Arabic ʿaql bi-l-quwwa, ʿaql bi-l-fiʿl, ʿaql mustafād and ʿaql faʿʿāl, noting that al-Kindī, like al-Fārābī, names Aristotle as author of the division.

src.l: al-Kindī, 1897, Die philosophischen Abhandlungen des al-Kindi

s: Avicenna's De anima (Latin) holds that the human soul is first intelligent in potency and becomes intelligent in act only through a cause that has the intelligible forms in act, the agent intelligence, whose relation to our souls is like the sun's to our sight.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.loc: De anima V.5, 'Capitulum de intelligentia agente in nostris animabus' [scan 90]
src.q: We say that the human soul is first intelligent in potency, then it becomes intelligent in act. Everything, however, which exits from potency to act does not exit except through a cause which has that thing in act and draws it out to it.
src.qo: Sed causa dandi forma intelligibilem non est in hi intelligentia in effectu. penes quam sunt incepta formarum intelligibilium abstractarum.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: Whose comparison to our souls is like the cooperation of the sun to our sights

s: For Avicenna (Latin De anima) learning is nothing other than acquiring the perfect aptitude to be joined to the agent intelligence, from which intelligible forms emanate into the soul; knowledge is not stored in the individual soul but received from an intellect outside it.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), 1500, De anima (Liber sextus de naturalibus), Latin
src.q: to learn is nothing other than to acquire the perfect aptitude to be joined to the agent intelligence, until there is made from it an intellect which is simple, from which ordered forms emanate into the soul in thought.

s: In al-Fārābī's Virtuous City (Dieterici's German), the active intellect is the cause by which potential intelligibles become actual and the potential intellect becomes actual, and what the thinking faculty receives from it stands to it as a ray of light to the eye.

src.l: al-Fārābī, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1900, Der Musterstaat von Alfarabi
src.loc: ch. XXIVa 'Der schaffende Intellect, die Denk- und Vorstellungskraft', Dieterici p. 80 [scan 172]
src.q: The active intellect is the cause through which that which is only a potential intelligible becomes an actual intelligible, and also the cause for the potential intellect becoming actual.
src.qo: Der schaffende Intellect ist die Ursache, durch die das nur potentiell Intelligibile zum actuellen Intelligibile wird, auch dafür dass der potentielle Intellect zum actuellen wird.

src.l: al-Fārābī, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1900, Der Musterstaat von Alfarabi

s: Al-Fārābī (Virtuous City, Dieterici) ranks the intellects as a ladder of matter and form: the natural disposition is substrate for the passive intellect, the passive for the acquired intellect, and the acquired for the active intellect, with nothing between the acquired and the active intellect.

src.l: al-Fārābī, Friedrich Dieterici (trans.), 1900, Der Musterstaat von Alfarabi
src.q: It stands between the passive intellect and the agent intellect. Nothing else lies between it and the agent intellect. The passive intellect is thus like matter and a substrate for the acquired intellect, and this latter is in turn like matter and a substrate for the agent intellect.
src.qo: Derselbe wird dann benannt »der gewonnene (erworbene) Intellect«. Er steht zwischen dem Passiv-Intellect und dem schaffenden Intellect. Nichts andres liegt zwischen ihm und dem schaffenden Intellect.

s: Al-Fārābī (Virtuous City, Dieterici) says that when the active intellect dwells in a man in both parts of his thinking faculty and in his imagination, God grants him revelation through it: the emanation to his passive intellect makes him a philosopher, the emanation to his imagination a prophet.

src.q: Through the outpouring from that passive intellect, the human being becomes a wise man, a philosopher, and one who adheres to perfection. ... he becomes a prophet, a warner of what is to come

s: Against the unity of the possible intellect, Aquinas (De spiritualibus creaturis a. 9) argues that if men understand by the possible intellect and it is one for all, then what one man understands another understands, which is plainly false; and since the intellectual soul is form and mover of a determinate body, one soul cannot serve many humans.

s: In the Mishkāt al-anwār (Gairdner's English), al-Ghazālī holds that the intelligence errs only through the imaginative and phantastic faculties: separated from them it sees things as they are, a separation that is difficult and perfected only after death.

src.l: al-Ghazālī, W. H. T. Gairdner (trans.), 1924, Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche for Lights)
src.q: But when the intelligence is separated from the deceptions of the phantasy and the imagination, error on its part is inconceivable; it sees things as they are. This separation is, however, difficult, and only attains perfection after death.

s: In Guide I.68 Maimonides concludes that because God is intellect always in act, with no potentiality, He and what He apprehends are one, so that God is perpetually 'the Intellect, the Thinker, and the Object Understood' (Intellectus, Intelligens & Intellectum).

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (trans.), 1629, Liber More Nevuchim, Doctor perplexorum

s: Guide I.68 states the identity as general: in everything understood in act, the intellect, the thinker and the object understood are one; only in potentiality are they two.

s: Against any easy analogy between Maimonides' intellect and AI: in Guide I.1 the very mark that makes intellect God's image is that it 'does not require any physical sense or the work of the body' and is in no bodily instrument, while a machine's cognition is nothing but instrument; and the likeness even to God is said to hold only κατὰ δόξαν, not truly.

s: In Consolation V pr. 4 Boethius ranks four modes of cognition by object: sense grasps figure in matter, imagination figure without matter, reason (ratio) the universal, and intelligence (intelligentia) the pure form itself.

src.l: Boethius, 1501, De consolatione philosophiae
src.q: Sense judges figure clothed in material substance, Imagination figure alone without matter. Thought transcends this again, and by its contemplation of universals considers the type itself which is contained in the individual. The eye of Intelligence is yet more exalted

s: Boethius assigns sense alone to immobile creatures, imagination to animals that move, reason to the human race only, and intelligence to the divine alone; the higher power knows the objects of the lower as well as its own.

src.l: Boethius, 1501, De consolatione philosophiae
src.q: Thought pertains only to the human race, as Intelligence to Divinity alone ; hence it follows that that form of knowledge exceeds the rest which of its own nature cognizes not only its proper object, but the objects of the other forms of knowledge also.

s: Boethius diagnoses the foreknowledge problem as human reason measuring divine intelligence by its own mode of knowing; the solution is to rise to the higher power's standpoint.

src.l: Boethius, 1501, De consolatione philosophiae
src.q: human reason thinks that Divine Intelligence cannot see the future except after the fashion in which its own knowledge is obtained.

s: Galton defined the 'natural ability' whose inheritance Hereditary Genius studies as a compound of intellect and disposition: neither capacity without zeal, nor zeal without capacity, nor both without the power of sustained hard work.

src.l: Francis Galton, 1869, Hereditary Genius: An Inquiry into its Laws and Consequences
src.loc: 1869 ed., pp. 37-38 (definition of reputation and natural ability)

s: The book that defines 'natural ability' frames it in hereditarian and racial ranking: its contents list a chapter 'The Comparative Worth of Different Races', and it ranks men 'into classes separated by equal degrees of merit'; any use of Galton's integrated notion of ability inherits this frame.

src.l: Francis Galton, 1869, Hereditary Genius: An Inquiry into its Laws and Consequences
src.loc: 1869 ed., table of contents; chapter ranking men by natural ability

s: Binet and Simon (1905) held that intelligence has one fundamental faculty, judgment, glossed as good sense, practical sense, initiative and the faculty of adapting oneself to circumstances, beside which the other intellectual faculties matter little.

src.l: Alfred Binet, Théodore Simon, 1905, Méthodes nouvelles pour le diagnostic du niveau intellectuel des anormaux
src.loc: 'New Methods', opening section on the definition of intelligence (Kite tr. 1916)

s: Spearman (1904) concluded from correlations among school marks and sensory discrimination that all branches of intellectual activity share one fundamental function (or group of functions), with the remaining specific elements wholly different in each, the general-to-specific ratio running from 15:1 to 1:4 across ten departments.

src.l: Charles Spearman, 1904, "General Intelligence," Objectively Determined and Measured
src.loc: Ch. V, Conclusions, point IV (contents: 'Universal Unity of the Intellective Function', p. 272)

s: Legg and Hutter's collection attributes to Boring (1923, 'Intelligence as the tests test it', New Republic) the operational definition that intelligence is what intelligence tests measure.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence

s: Burt's definition, as collected by Legg and Hutter, makes intelligence intellectual 'and not emotional or moral' and tries to rule out zeal, interest and industry in measuring it, the exact components Galton had built into natural ability and that a harmonizing account of intelligence would include.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence
src.loc: §3 Psychologist definitions, no. 6 (Burt, The causes and treatments of backwardness, 1957)

s: Piaget's definition, as collected by Legg and Hutter, makes intelligence both assimilation of experience into existing schemata and accommodation to the environment, the schemata being constantly modified to adjust to new elements.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence
src.loc: §3 Psychologist definitions, no. 22 (Piaget, The psychology of intelligence, 1963 English ed.)

s: Peterson's definition, quoted in Sternberg's Handbook of Intelligence and collected by Legg and Hutter, makes intelligence the biological mechanism that brings the effects of many stimuli together into a somewhat unified effect in behaviour.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence
src.loc: §3 Psychologist definitions, no. 24 ('J. Peterson quoted in' Sternberg ed. 2000)

s: Thurstone's definition, as collected by Legg and Hutter, makes intelligence include the capacity to realise the modified instinctive adjustment in behaviour to the advantage of the individual as a social animal.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence
src.loc: §3 Psychologist definitions, nos. 30-31 (Thurstone, The nature of intelligence, 1924; and quoted in Sternberg ed. 2000)

s: Sternberg, in an interview collected by Legg and Hutter, defines 'successful intelligence' as skill in achieving whatever one wants to attain in life within one's sociocultural context.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence
src.loc: §3 Psychologist definitions, no. 27 (Sternberg interview in Plucker ed.)

s: Wechsler's definition, as collected by Legg and Hutter from the 4th (1958) edition of The Measurement and Appraisal of Adult Intelligence, calls intelligence a global concept involving the ability to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence

s: The 1994 'Mainstream Science on Intelligence' statement (reprinted with 52 signatories, Gottfredson 1997) defines intelligence as a very general mental capability involving reasoning, planning, problem solving, abstract thought, comprehension of complex ideas and quick learning from experience, and says it is not merely book learning or test-taking smarts.

src.l: Linda S. Gottfredson, 1997, Mainstream Science on Intelligence: An Editorial with 52 Signatories, History, and Bibliography
src.loc: statement, item 1 ('The Meaning and Measurement of Intelligence')

s: Turing (1950) declined to define 'machine' and 'think', replaced 'Can machines think?' with the imitation game, judged the original question 'too meaningless to deserve discussion', and predicted that by the century's end one could speak of machines thinking without being contradicted.

Alan M. Turing, 1950, Computing Machinery and Intelligence

src.l: Alan M. Turing, 1950, Computing Machinery and Intelligence

src.l: John R. Searle, 1980, Minds, Brains, and Programs
src.loc: p. 418 (reply to the first claim of strong AI)

s: Legg and Hutter collected some 70 informal definitions of intelligence and distilled them into one: intelligence measures an agent's ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments, with learning and adaptation implicit.

src.l: Shane Legg, Marcus Hutter, 2007, A Collection of Definitions of Intelligence

s: Chollet (2019) argues that skill at given tasks cannot measure intelligence because priors and training data can buy arbitrary skill, defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency over a scope of tasks relative to priors, experience and generalization difficulty, and proposes ARC (400 training and 600 evaluation tasks) built on Core Knowledge priors.

src.l: François Chollet, 2019, On the Measure of Intelligence
François Chollet, 2019, On the Measure of Intelligence

s: Bostrom's orthogonality thesis takes intelligence roughly as the capacity for instrumental reasoning and holds that intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes: more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.

src.l: Nick Bostrom, 2012, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents

s: Omohundro (2008) argues that sufficiently advanced goal-seeking systems of any design will have drives (self-improvement, rationality, protection of their utility functions, self-preservation, resource acquisition) unless explicitly counteracted, and Bostrom formalizes this as the instrumental convergence thesis.

src.l: Stephen M. Omohundro, 2008, The Basic AI Drives
Nick Bostrom, 2012, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents

s: Omohundro predicts that advanced AI architectures will face internal tensions and will want subcomponents that explore varied strategies while the system acts 'as a coherent harmonious whole', policed against internal corruption; this internal harmony serves the system's own utility function, whatever it is.

src.l: Stephen M. Omohundro, 2008, The Basic AI Drives

s: Read together, the orthogonality thesis and Omohundro's drives press on definitions that build integration, social advantage or the good into intelligence: if intelligence is instrumental reasoning compatible with any final goal, and internal coherence is instrumentally useful to any goal, then integrating motives into coherent action is not yet integrating them toward the good of the whole.

src.l: Nick Bostrom, 2012, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents
Stephen M. Omohundro, 2008, The Basic AI Drives

s: Against 'intelligence is the harmonizing': the Indian texts that prize a single, unified intellect reach unity by restraint and exclusion (withdrawing the senses like a tortoise, hindering citta's modifications, making mind motionless until 'mindlessness'), not by integrating diverse motives into coherent action; the many-branched intellects are cut away, not reconciled.
